newsitem.title: GREECE: HARD DRACHMA POLICY UNSUSTAINABLE, SEEN WEAK-EIU.
newsitem.headline: HARD DRACHMA POLICY UNSUSTAINABLE, SEEN WEAK-EIU.

text.p: Greece's widening current account deficit is likely to pull the carpet under the central bank's hard drachma policy and make it unsustainable, the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) said in its 1997-98 outlook on Greece.

"With a current account deficit which has risen to $4.5 billion or 3.7 percent of GDP in 1996 and which is expected to deteriorate further, the hard drachma policy is unlikely to be sustainable," the EIU said.
The report forecast a substantial depreciation of the drachma against the core EU currencies in 1998 and against the euro in 1999, assuming that EMU does go ahead.
After a delay, this will benefit the current account and stimulate growth through higher exports. But it will also slow down the decline in inflation, it said.
At present, the deficit is funded by inflows of mainly short-term capital, attracted by Greece's high interest rates or borrowing by Greek companies looking for lower interest rates overseas.

"But such capital flows add to the investment income deficit and cannot continue indefinitely. There will be some benefit to competitiveness from the recent strengthening of the dollar against the main EU currencies which has led to a decline in the drachma relative to the dollar," it said.
However, it is in European markets that Greece needs most crucially to regain competitiveness to boost its exports and limit its imports.

Real GDP growth which the government sees hitting 3.5 percent this year and 3.7 percent in 1998 looked "far too optimistic" on weaker private consumption growth in 1997-98, seen below the government forecast of 2.2 percent this year.
The EIU forecast for real GDP growth in 1997 is 2.6 percent, 2.5 percent in 1998.

And on the assumption that defence expenditure is not boosted significantly, it predicted a budget deficit of 5.0 percent of GDP in 1997 -- "a significant step in the right direction although above the 4.2 percent government target."

"Because of its determination to reduce administrative staff through a policy of hiring only one new employee for every five leaving and to eliminate special tax privileges, we expect that the government will bring the deficit down further to 4.0 percent in 1998," the EIU said.
This will put it in striking distance of achieving the 3.0 percent target in 1999, one year later than the government's own target date.

This will mainly be due to economic growth and therefore tax revenue growth which will turn out one percentage point below the government's 1997-98 projections. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
